subtopic: Responding to a natural disaster or accident
subtype: Approach: safety first and quick triage [Thinking]
passage:
Note for the school's flood-response wall, from the teacher who lives next door
On the night the canal overflowed, I watched Pradeep from my window. The water came into our lane fast, ankle-deep, then knee-deep. His parents were stuck at work across the city.
He didn't run for the TV or the fridge. Through the wall I heard him thinking out loud: “Things can be replaced. People first. Who's home? Dadi, Dadu, Pallavi.” He went room to room and counted them.
Then he took Dadu's arm on the stairs first, because Dadu walks slowest, and came back for Dadi. Pallavi carried the medicine box. Only when all three were upstairs in the terrace room did he go back down for the documents bag. He left the sofa and the TV to the water.
At midnight I called across to check. He answered, “All four of us upstairs. Dry.” I will tell his class teacher how calmly he handled it.

qa.a: Dadu, because Dadu walks slowest.

qa.q: What does Pradeep's thinking aloud suggest about his state of mind?
qa.a: It suggests he was frightened but focused, steadying himself by deciding clearly that people came before belongings.

qa.q: What else could Pradeep have done once everyone was upstairs?
qa.a: Call his parents and a helpline to say where they were, so help knew four people were on the upper floor.

qa.q: What might that night have been like for Pallavi?
qa.a: Pallavi probably felt scared, but safer with a job to do and someone deciding calmly.

Tuesday night, written by torchlight upstairs
The water came in at about four. I was alone with Aita and Ira; Ma and Deuta had gone to the market in town, and the road was cut.
My first thought was the new school bag, my books, the TV. Then I stopped myself on the stairs. Books dry. People don't. So: who is here? Aita, who can't climb fast. Ira, who is six and was still splashing like it was a game.
I got Ira up first and told her to sit on the top step and not move. Then Aita, one step at a time, her hand on my shoulder. Only then did I go down for the documents tin and Aita's tablets.
My bag is floating somewhere in the kitchen. I don't care. Everyone is upstairs.
Ma called on Aita's phone an hour ago; the village volunteers know we're here.
– Binita

qa.a: Aita was likely frightened and slow, but reassured by a steady shoulder to lean on, one step at a time.

subtopic: Responding to a natural disaster or accident

passage:
The fire alarm in our building went off at 9:40 one night last year. I'm Manoj, and the only reason I didn't freeze is that we had practised this exact thing at home after the school drill in June.
Papa shouted from the balcony, “Smoke from the floor below. Plan!” My part of the plan was simple, because we'd said it out loud so many times. I grabbed the red bag from behind the door: our documents in a plastic folder, the torch, water, Papa's tablets. Papa told me to switch off the mains, and I did it at the switch box by the kitchen, just as we'd practised, only because he said to. We took the stairs, not the lift, Mummy holding my sister's hand.
The meeting point was the gate by the temple. Baljeet's family was already there. We counted: four of us. Everyone.
The fire was small in the end. But my hands only stopped shaking when I counted four.

qa.q: What was in the red bag?
qa.a: The documents in a plastic folder, the torch, water and Papa's tablets.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling until the family was counted at the gate?
qa.a: Manoj was frightened, hands shaking, and only felt relief after counting all four of them.

qa.q: What else could the family add to the plan after this night?
qa.a: Practise it together again and check the red bag every few months, so everything inside is still there and up to date.

qa.q: How might Baljeet's family have seen Manoj's family arrive?
qa.a: They would likely be relieved to see all four safe at the gate, and glad both families knew the same meeting point.

grounding: Shows a teen following a family plan practised after school drills: taking the emergency bag, switching off the mains when told, and going to the meeting point.

Parent's note for the school's safety week display
When the landslide siren sounded in our village above Munnar on Saturday night, I watched our son Jomon do exactly what his school had drilled. He took the green emergency bag from the hook without being told: the documents pouch, the torch, the whistle, dry biscuits. I asked him to switch off the mains at the board by the door, and he did, then checked the gas knob too, as we had shown him. He held his sister Rajni's hand and walked with her down the path to the church hall, the meeting point we had agreed after the June drill.
At the hall he counted us and told the volunteer our names and how many we were. The slope held that night, and we went home the next afternoon.
I am writing this because I was the one shaking. He was calm, because he had practised.

Teacher's note, Wednesday, incident near the school gate
At 3:15 a scooter and an autorickshaw collided at the corner outside our gate. I reached the gate a minute later, and by then Ramesh from Class Ten was already on the phone to the emergency number, standing on the footpath well back from the road.
I heard him clearly: “There's an accident at the corner of MG Road and Station Road, outside the main gate of Sunrise School. Two people are hurt. The scooter rider is on the ground and not getting up; the auto driver is sitting and bleeding from his arm. It happened one minute ago.” Then: “Yes, I'll stay on the line.”
He told his classmate Pooja to stop other students crowding the road, and he did not go near the traffic himself. He answered every question until the ambulance arrived, eleven minutes later.
I have told his parents and the principal how well he handled it.

Friday
Still shaky. After school, at the bus stop on Canal Road, a car hit a boy on a cycle. He was lying on the road holding his leg. Everyone just stared. Ojas started running toward him, into the traffic, and I grabbed his bag and pulled him back. “Cars!”
Then I called the emergency number. I made myself say it the way we learnt in the safety class: where, how many, what happened. “Bus stop on Canal Road, opposite the petrol pump. One boy hurt, he was on a cycle, hit by a car. He's awake, holding his leg.” The woman on the phone asked me to stay on the line and tell her if anything changed. I did, from the footpath.
The ambulance came in about ten minutes. A shopkeeper stood with the boy until it did.
I only realised afterwards how hard my heart was beating.
– Vijay

subtopic: Responding to a natural disaster or accident

passage:
Dear Jatin Sir,
You told us at the end of the school first aid course to write if we ever used it. On Sunday I did.
My uncle was fixing the fan on the verandah when the ladder slipped. He fell and hit the railing. His forearm was cut and bleeding a lot, and he said his neck hurt.
I remembered two things you drilled into us. First, pressure. I folded a clean towel, pressed it hard on the cut and kept pressing, even when it soaked through; I put a second towel on top instead of lifting the first. Second, don't move someone who might have a neck injury. He wanted to sit up. I said, “Please stay still, Uncle, the ambulance is coming,” and kept talking to him about cricket to keep him calm. My aunt called the ambulance.
The doctors said his neck was only bruised. But they were glad nobody moved him.
Thank you, Sir.
Thomas

qa.q: What did Thomas do when the first towel soaked through?
qa.a: Put a second towel on top instead of lifting the first.

qa.q: What was Thomas probably feeling when the uncle wanted to sit up?
qa.a: Thomas was likely scared of doing harm but determined, gently keeping the uncle still and calm.

qa.q: Why is staying within trained limits important in a moment like this?
qa.a: Doing only what the course taught, pressure and keeping still, helps without risking harm while professionals handle the rest.

qa.q: How might Jatin Sir feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Jatin Sir would likely feel proud and moved that the course helped a student act calmly in a real emergency.

grounding: Shows a teen trained in school first aid pressing on a bleeding cut, keeping the injured person calm and still, and not moving someone with a possible neck injury.

Aadhya, you asked what the first aid course was actually good for. I'm Kamal, and I'll tell you about last Saturday in the park.
A man on a cycle hit the kerb near the gate and went over the handlebars. When I got there, his palm was cut deep and bleeding, and he was lying still, saying his neck felt strange.
I didn't try to be a doctor. I did the two things the course said. I pressed my clean handkerchief on his palm, hard, and held it, and when it soaked through I added my scarf on top without lifting. And I didn't let anyone move him. A man wanted to sit him up against the wall, and I said, “No, his neck, please wait for the ambulance.” My friend called the ambulance; I kept talking to him, asking about his dog, just to keep him calm and still.
Then the paramedics took over. That's it. That's what it's good for.

Dear Charu,
You asked if we felt the earthquake in Guwahati. We did. And I did everything wrong.
I was on my bed scrolling when it started to shake. I actually thought, it's a truck passing, and kept watching the video. Then the ceiling fan swung and the glass on my table fell. Even then I just sat there with the phone in my hand. My head was completely blank. We'd never practised anything at home, and all I could think was, what do I do?
Ma screamed my name from the corridor. By the time I moved, the shaking was nearly over. The bookshelf beside my bed had tipped over onto the mattress where my legs had been a second before.
Nobody was hurt. But I lost maybe fifteen seconds just staring.
This weekend Ma and I are making a plan and practising it. Want me to send it to you?
Jaya

qa.a: A truck passing.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling as the fan swung?
qa.a: Jaya felt frozen and confused, mind completely blank, with no practised action to fall back on.

qa.q: What could Jaya's family do before another tremor?

qa.a: Ma was probably terrified, and later shaken to see the bookshelf on the mattress where Jaya had been.

Rajni, you asked why I'm so strict about our earthquake drill now. I'm Urmila, and it's because of Dharamshala, last March.
We were in the hostel study room. The table began to tremble and a pen rolled off. Everyone looked up, and I looked back down at my phone. I honestly thought, that's nothing, someone's jumping upstairs. I kept scrolling. Then the windows rattled, and the girl next to me was already under the table, and I was still sitting there holding the phone, with no idea what to do. Not a single step came into my head. We'd never practised in that building.
It stopped after maybe twenty seconds. The big wall clock came down right behind my chair.
Nothing happened to me. But I wasted those seconds. So now, when the warden calls a drill, I'm first under the table, and I make you do it too.

passage:
I'm Mehak, and I was on our terrace when it happened. The river had burst into the lower lane that afternoon, brown and fast. Damini's dog, Moti, was stranded on a cart that was turning slowly in the current.
Damini came down the steps shouting his name. Her father was on the phone with the rescue team, telling her to wait. She didn't. She walked straight in. For three steps the water was at her knees; then at her waist, and I saw her feet go out from under her.
Two men from the tea stall grabbed a rope and pulled her back to the steps. One of them was swept against a pole and cut his arm. The rescue boat arrived twenty minutes later, as promised, and lifted Moti off the cart easily.
Damini sat on the steps, soaked and shaking, holding the dog. I don't know if she was angry or ashamed. She didn't say anything for a long time.

qa.a: Twenty minutes later, as promised.

qa.a: Damini was probably desperate and panicked for Moti, too frightened for the dog to think about the current.

qa.q: What would have been safer for Damini to do?
qa.a: Stay on the steps with her father, keep an eye on Moti, and let the rescue team, already called, reach him by boat.

qa.q: How was the rescue for the men from the tea stall?

subtopic: Responding to a natural disaster or accident
subtype: Approach: spreading unverified messages [Pitfall]
passage:
When the cyclone warning came for our coast last year, I did something I'm still embarrassed about. I'm Chandrika. A message landed in our building's group: “URGENT evacuation route: take Beach Road to the college shelter.” It had a map, lots of red, and “forward to everyone”. It looked official. I forwarded it to four groups within a minute.
It was wrong. Beach Road was the one road the district office had closed, and the college wasn't a shelter that year. Francis Uncle from the second floor packed his elderly mother into an auto and headed for Beach Road. Police turned them back at the barrier, and they lost almost an hour in the rain reaching the right shelter at the school.
Later I found the real route on the district office's page in two minutes. Two minutes I hadn't spent.
Now, before I forward anything in an emergency, I check the official page or the radio first. If I can't check it, I don't send it.

qa.q: How many groups did Chandrika forward the message to?
qa.a: Four groups, within a minute.

qa.q: How does Chandrika feel looking back on forwarding it?
qa.a: Chandrika still feels embarrassed, knowing two minutes of checking could have spared Francis Uncle an hour in the rain.

qa.q: What rule does Chandrika follow now, and why does it help?
qa.a: Check the official page or the radio before forwarding in an emergency, so only confirmed routes spread.

qa.q: What was the evening like for Francis Uncle?
qa.a: Francis Uncle, with his elderly mother in an auto, was turned back at the barrier and lost almost an hour in the rain.

passage:
Class teacher's note, after the cyclone holiday
On the evening of the warning I saw it happen in our class parents' group. Dolma, whose mother had added her to the group, forwarded a message saying the cyclone would hit at 2 am and that everyone near the market should go to the old bus stand. It carried no source.
Within twenty minutes, Lavanya's mother wrote that she was packing to leave. The old bus stand was low-lying; the district office's actual shelter was the high school. I posted the official page link and asked everyone to follow only that.
When school reopened, Dolma came to me before assembly, very quiet. She said she'd thought she was helping. We looked together at how to find the district office's updates and the weather department's page, and what a source line looks like.
Dolma asked if she could explain this to the class herself. I have said yes, for Friday.

subtopic: Responding to a natural disaster or accident
subtype: Approach: contingency planning for communication [Thinking]
passage:
Sunday
Family meeting after dinner, because of the flood warnings. Papa asked, “If the phones stop working, how do we find each other?” Nobody had an answer. I realised all our numbers live only inside our phones. If my battery dies, I don't even know Mummy's number by heart.
So we decided:
1. If the networks fail and we're apart, everyone goes to the community hall near the water tank. We wait there.
2. Everyone contacts Mausi in Pune, because a far-away line may work when local ones are jammed. She becomes our message centre.
3. I write the important numbers on paper.
Damini Didi said paper is old-fashioned. I said paper doesn't run out of battery. She laughed and agreed.
I've made four small cards: Papa, Mummy, Didi, Mausi and the hall address. One in each school bag, one in Papa's wallet, one on the fridge.
– Mridul

passage:
The plan was simple: if the river rose, Bhavna would take her little brother Sumit up the temple path to the school on the hill, where the family would meet. But when they reached the bend, a landslip had buried the path under mud and rocks.
Sumit started to cry. Bhavna's heart was pounding, but she crouched and held his shoulders. “We'll find another way.”
Two panchayat volunteers in orange vests stood at the bend, turning people back. “Go round by the fields and the water tank,” one said. “It's longer but it's safe; we checked it an hour ago.”
Bhavna nodded and took the fields path, holding Sumit's hand. On the way she messaged the family group from Ma's old phone: “Temple path blocked. Going by the water tank. Meet at the school's side gate, not the front.”
Forty minutes later, Ma and Baba were waiting at the side gate.

Wednesday
Day three of the school relief drive. Sachin wanted to take the bus to the flooded villages himself with a bag of biscuits. I almost went with him. Then Mrs Kulkarni said the roads there are still unsafe and the district team decides where things go, so we can do more good here.
So here's what I did today, 2 to 6 pm, in the school hall with Mrs Kulkarni watching over us: sorted three cartons of clothes by size, checked every food packet for its expiry date, and typed up the list of what came in, so the district team knows exactly what's on the truck. 146 items today.
Boring? A bit. But at 5:30 the truck left with everything labelled, and the driver said the camp can hand things out in minutes because of the lists.
Sachin did the lists with me in the end. He said it felt less heroic, but more useful.
– Vinita
